items.summary: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
items.title: Geometric Refinement and Distributional Alignment for Sim2Real Roadside LiDAR Detection

items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. The isolated Kalman filter (IsoKF) of Jung, Luft and Weiss (Autonomous Robots, 2025) lets the nodes of a robot or sensor network share an estimation task cheaply: only the nodes involved in a measurement update, and their correlations with everyone else are rescaled by a correction factor. Its authors conjectured that for any completely observable and controllable system the covariance it reports converges to a finite, unique, stable steady state. Result: the conjecture is false. A three-node system with pair-sum observations x1+x2, x2+x3, x3+x1 and dynamics A = 3I is observable from one epoch and controllable, every local block the filter uses stays positive definite, yet the reported marginal variances satisfy m_k ≥ (5/4)(9/5)^k − 1/4, while the centralised Kalman filter keeps every variance at most 3/4. A Perron-root comparison extends divergence to every connected non-bipartite pair-sum graph when a^2 is large enough; extra attenuation or deletion of cross-covariances does not help. Schur-stable dynamics always give bounded marginals (proved). Computer-assisted proofs (outward-rounded interval arithmetic) show that for a^2 in (1, 1.38] large priors diverge at rate a^(2k), entry certified from 10^12 I at eight values down to a^2 = 1 + 10^-8, and that at a^2 = 21/20 the prior I converges while 10^12 I diverges: there is no globally attracting steady covariance. Also: exact classification of participant overlaps (|U ∩ V| ≤ 1) that keep every local block positive definite, and a bounded regime for anchored relative measurements. Scope: in high-precision numerical tests the actual estimation error stays bounded; the failure is gross pessimism of the reported covariance, not divergence of the estimate. The counterexample uses pair-sum measurements, not plain differences. Nothing is proved for a^2 in (1.38, 2+√5); uniqueness for stable dynamics remains open. The ikf_lib software was inspected but not run; no software failure is claimed. Version 0.2.0 (correction). Version 0.1.0 compared this work with Luft, Schubert, Roumeliotis and Burgard (2018, IJRR, doi:10.1177/0278364918760698) at abstract level only. This version compares it with the full text: Luft et al. introduce the correction factor (their eq. 26) and a scaled variant (eq. 28), and prove that two-robot blocks stay positive definite (Proposition 1, now credited at Theorem 8.1 and Corollary 5.3); they make no claim about boundedness or convergence of the covariance and give no divergence example. The two citing works are now also compared in full text. No theorem, proof, certificate, computation or numerical finding changed. Archive: LaTeX manuscript and PDF, bibliography with registry records, exact rational verifiers, interval certificates C1–C3, numerical scripts and their outputs (normal and python -O), figures, CI and SHA-256 manifest. Assurance: internal AI-assisted review only (not human peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification); certificates are computer-assisted, not formal proofs. Creator: Anonymous. Text CC0-1.0; code MIT.

items.summary: Sensor fusion, data fusion, dashboards and data visualisation are conventionally distinguished by input type and by where they sit in a processing stack. This paper argues that the distinction which matters for decision quality is a different one, and that it is two variables applied to all four: every representation of multi-source evidence collapses a distribution somewhere between sensor and decision, and representations differ in the locus of that collapse and in whether the residual uncertainty survives it as a carried object. Fusion collapses upstream and, when honest, ships the residual as covariance or hypothesis mass. Dashboards defer collapse to the viewer's retina and ship nothing; the resulting belief has no bookkeeping. Visualisation is the encoding of whichever object arrives, indifferent to whether it is a point or a distribution, which is why it is blamed for collapses committed upstream. The two variables, collapse locus and residual retention, place the four terms on one map, generalise the confabulation coefficient of The Confabulating Collator from language-model collators to the whole representation stack, and yield a diagnostic: the failure mode conventionally called bad fusion is a product that collapsed upstream and discarded its residual, delivering the confidence of a posterior with the epistemic hygiene of a gauge. The publicly reported expectation, in the investigation of the February 2026 Minab strike, that a targeting platform would have flagged contradictions it carried no representation of, is read as this failure at operational scale, with the causal question left where the public record leaves it. A design rule follows: defer collapse to the human where the human carries the prior the system lacks, fuse where they do not, and at neither locus discard the residual. The constructive requirement for language-level fusion products is stated and handed to a companion paper on divergence retention. The operator located in the architecture is Binary Bias.
items.title: Where the Cloud Collapses

items.summary: Supplementary material and reproducibility package for the article Probing Coherent Noise with Stabilizer Codes: Identifiability, Ambiguity, and Decoder Priors . The supplement analyses the null result of a recent repetition-code experiment (arXiv:2606.07377), in which the logical fidelity of d = 3 and d = 5 bit-flip repetition codes was found to be indistinguishable under coherent and stochastic error injection, contrary to the circuit-level simulation of that work. It establishes three results, each independently checkable: The average gate infidelity of a coherent rotation is exactly invariant under randomization of its rotation axis by a drifting frame phase, so no fidelity-based comparison can detect such randomization at all. For a bit-flip repetition code read out in the computational basis, an X-type coherent injection and a stochastic injection of equal single-site average fidelity give logical error probabilities that agree to machine precision (3×10 −15 ), for d = 3 and d = 5, R = 10 rounds, with and without syndrome misreports. The gap reported in the experiment therefore cannot originate in coherent accumulation on the data qubits. The coherent–stochastic gap obeys [1 + (N−1)ρ]/N with ρ = <cos Δφ> = exp(−σ φ 2 ). The frame-phase spread required for the drift hypothesis to apply (σ φ ≳ 1.5 rad) lies a factor 30 outside the parameter domain of the generator model and an order of magnitude outside the small-angle domain in which the leading-order polarization expansion is formulated. The role of the companion's channel-level generator recovery is stated explicitly, in a dedicated section: it supplies the parameter (a static frame offset is δ i , with |δ i | ≤ 0.05 rad), the ε 2 /ε 4 order counting that makes the code orientation a choice of sensitivity, and the estimator itself; this note supplies the temporal question that the companion does not answer. The role of the companion's channel-level generator recovery is stated explicitly, in a dedicated section: it supplies the parameter (a static frame offset is delta_i, with |delta_i| <= 0.05 rad), the eps^2/eps^4 order counting that makes the code orientation a choice of sensitivity, and the estimator itself; this note supplies the temporal question that the companion does not answer. The supplement closes with a channel-level ratio, coh(R_code)/coh(R_ref), that would settle the question with data of the size already recorded. Contents. supplementary_material.pdf (9 pp., 5 figures, 2 tables) and its LaTeX source; five 400 dpi figures; Python code (numpy / scipy / matplotlib) that regenerates every figure and every quoted number from a single entry point; all generated data files in JSON; README with the model assumptions, the limitations, and the relation to the two source papers. Code is released under the MIT licence; text, figures and data under CC BY 4.0.

items.summary: Classical creative-process orderings put divergence early and convergence late, and the Double Diamond formalises the rule twice over. This paper argues the ordering was never a law of cognition but a map of costs: divergence goes early because reopening a converged process has historically been ruinous, and the entire discipline of the framework exists to protect against that reopening. When drafting cost collapses by orders of magnitude, as it does when an author works with a language model as typewriter, the protected assumption dissolves and the optimal ordering inverts: converge first, then diverge, because a late horizon either restarts a now-cheap process or spawns a child concept from a sharpened parent. The paper's second claim types reviewer instances in multi-model chains by regression target rather than capability, and states the Hein Condition: a mode-regressing reviewer's yield is proportional to the sharpness of the artefact it receives, because the modal response to an unsharp artefact is the generic response, so the same instance is most fluent exactly where it is least useful. A slot theory follows, carnivore, auditor, mode-regressor, children, each reviewer placed where its failure mode is cheapest, and child viability rises with parent sharpness at spawn. The claims are exercised on a fully documented case: a five-pass, three-model review chain run on a single paper in a single day, with every absorption, declination, and provenance failure logged. Four predictions close, including that review chains are provenance systems measurable by the sibling paper's key-inflation ratio.
items.title: The Hein Condition

items.summary: Scientific agents can find interventions that work without understanding why they do. We study this failure mode in controlled synthetic regulatory systems, where agents must experimentally identify a hidden fault and rescue the resulting phenotype. Across seven LLMs, every model restores the healthy phenotypes more often than it identifies the fault. Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 rescue every organism while diagnosing only 55% and 35% of them. This failure is not simply due to insufficient exploration or unavailable evidence. In most cases, the cause is experimentally identifiable, and agents encounter evidence that distinguishes competing causes in 91% of relevant sessions, and still frequently misdiagnose the system. Targeted probes reveal where experimental reasoning breaks down. Models reliably interpret decisive evidence and revise hypotheses when the causal comparison is explicit, and can locate that evidence within a full experimental record. However, they struggle to predict the outcome of the experiment under each competing cause, a necessary step in using the observed result to distinguish between them. Agents can therefore gather the right evidence and still infer the wrong cause. As AI systems take on a growing role in synthesising scientific evidence, these findings highlight the need to evaluate how they use evidence to reach causal conclusions, alongside whether their interventions succeed.
items.title: Treating the Symptom, Missing the Cause: Anatomy of a Scientific Reasoning Failure

items.summary: On a public agent leaderboard, a general-purpose agent trails a scaffold built for an airline customer-service benchmark by 13 points on the tasks that touch its database, and a reader could conclude that generality costs accuracy. The gap comes from the grader. The general agent often ends its conversations in a way that never triggers grading, so only about half of its episodes were scored and the rest were stored as failures. Grading the ungraded half under the benchmark's own rule closes the pooled gap, without rerunning any agent. We audit two carefully maintained public leaderboards, HAL and tau2-bench, from their published artifacts alone and find three more instrument errors. A cost column counts nested model calls twice, unevenly across rows. Archived trajectories record grader-written actions as agent actions. Re-grading saved trajectories under a newer evaluator is itself a new measurement: a correct and announced fix reorders a leaderboard, and a mode check that misreads four files collapses their scores by 59 to 82 points while printing no error. Each produced a plausible number, and the HAL maintainers confirmed their three within five weeks. Together the cases show that the infrastructure of agent evaluation, meaning the code that grades, logs, replays and versions an evaluation, is part of the measurement and fails silently, so scores and orderings can move with no visible sign. These failure modes follow from how agent evaluation pipelines are built, and those pipelines change as fast as the agents they measure, so we expect more of them elsewhere. We propose cheap checks that expose the instrument: report the graded fraction, aggregate cost from root spans, tag the provenance of every recorded action, and pin evaluator versions with a published re-grade diff.
items.title: Silent Instrument Errors Reorder Agent Leaderboards

items.summary: Real-world geospatial decision support requires more than single-step retrieval or code generation. Disaster-response questions often involve multi-source workflows that combine spatial databases, map-derived features, satellite imagery, raster products, and reusable geospatial artifacts, where correctness depends on preserving spatial scope, temporal context, and intermediate execution state. While large language models and coding agents offer a promising interface for such workflows, they struggle with geospatial-specific failure modes, including handling large artifacts, selecting the wrong evidence source, losing spatial or temporal metadata, and applying invalid geometric operations. We introduce GeoFaham, a domain-specialized multi-agent system for geospatial disaster analytics. GeoFaham decomposes workflows into specialist agents for vector operations, map feature retrieval, imagery discovery, and raster analysis, coordinated by an Orchestrator with a dual-ledger control loop for dependency-aware planning, progress tracking, validation, and replanning. To support artifact-centric collaboration, GeoFaham uses a Response Store that persists full geospatial outputs and typed metadata outside the LLM context window while agents exchange compact identifiers and summaries. We also introduce GeoFaham-Bench, a 40-task benchmark grounded in 17 real-world disaster records, designed to evaluate multi-step geospatial reasoning, cross-source integration, raster-vector computation, artifact generation, and recovery under non-rigid ground truth. We evaluate GeoFaham on GeoFaham-Bench against strong general-purpose coding-agent baselines, including Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode. GeoFaham achieves the best overall performance, scoring 0.940 versus the next-best 0.879, while using 7.5 times fewer tokens. Our code and benchmark are publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/GeoFaham.
items.title: GeoFaham: Domain-Specialized Multi-Agent Geospatial Analytics for Disaster Response

items.summary: Measured failure modes of verifier panels: companion paper accepted (poster) at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop Who Verifies the Agents? — Verification Theater: Measured Failure Modes of AI Verifier Panels . Version of record: SSRN 7390698 , DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7390698 . Cite that version. The same text is also at https://polyhelper.ai/research/agreement-not-evidence/ and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/agreement-not-evidence . Someone who asks one language model a question cannot tell a confidently wrong answer from a confidently right one. The two are identical on every surface cue available to a non-expert. Asking several models seems to solve this, but it mostly relocates the problem: reconciling several answers produces one confident text again, and that text now carries the borrowed authority of "ten of them agreed." The protocol formalized here collects answers from several consumer chat models through the user's own browser or phone, with no API keys, no installation and no intermediary server. It reconciles them by anchor-and-enrich: the strongest available answer becomes the base, and each of the others contributes only what the base lacks. Every contribution is signed with the model that supplied it. Disagreements are kept in a section of their own rather than averaged away. The paper makes four contributions. The first is the protocol itself, stated as an algorithm that preserves provenance and forbids silent deletion, together with a taxonomy of five ways a merge can fail. Four of them are defects of naive pooling; the fifth is a failure of the operator rather than of the method: a synthesis that presents a single model's output as a collegial result. The second is the application of the correlated-witness arithmetic to protocol design. That arithmetic is not claimed here. Kohli (2026) applied the same Kish correction to a panel of nine frontier judges and measured about two effective votes, and Kim et al. (2025) established the underlying error correlation across more than 350 models. A council of N models whose errors carry intraclass correlation ρ is worth = N / (1 + (N−1)ρ) independent witnesses, and that quantity saturates at 1/ρ however many models are added. Once a council is larger than 1/ρ, halving ρ beats doubling N, and a pair with low error correlation can outweigh five with high correlation. Which pairs those are is measured, not read off the label: the larger and more accurate models carry the most correlated errors even when architecture and provider differ (Kim et al., 2025), and the author's per-pair measurements found no detectable effect of geopolitical bloc on error correlation and, in the pairs measured, none of shared lineage (Chernets, 2026). The estimation procedure of Section 5.5 supplies that measurement. The third is an account of three deployment tiers, manual, one-tap mobile and browser-agent, and of the axis that separates them epistemically: whether the second model sees the first model's answer. Conditioning the second model raises ρ in exchange for error correction. The fourth is a small-sample observation of the counterfeit-council failure across five models, the one-sentence intervention that removed it in a three-model re-run, and a blinded three-arm evaluation design with a stated falsification condition. Correlated agreement is treated here as established, not as a finding. That a panel of models is worth far fewer independent witnesses than it has members has been measured directly: nine frontier judges drawn from seven families supply about two effective votes (Kohli, 2026), and error correlation rises with model capability even across providers and architectures (Kim et al., 2025). Section 5 restates the design-effect arithmetic behind those measurements, because three of the protocol's rules are derived from it and read as fastidiousness without it. The protocol then takes the other side of the same problem. That literature measures the correlation; this protocol

items.summary: Wave energy converters (WECs) are typically designed to operate near resonance to maximize energy capture. While this enhances power absorption, it also amplifies structural loads and accelerates fatigue damage. As a result, fatigue becomes a critical design driver even when stress remains below material yield limits. Fatigue in offshore systems has been widely studied, particularly under variable-amplitude loading induced by waves, wind, and currents. These effects are commonly evaluated using the Palmgren–Miner damage accumulation rule, where failure is predicted once cumulative damage reaches unity. However, fatigue assessment for WECs remains less developed, especially in terms of linking environmental conditions to structural degradation and operational stress limits. The objective of this work is to evaluate, predict and improve confidence in the structural response and fatigue life of a WEC under representative operating conditions and to identify critical components and failure modes before deployment in March 2026 accounting for not only load and geometric factors, but also environmental conditions such as temperature.
items.title: Worst-Case Fatigue Life of an OSWEC Under Sustained Sea States

items.summary: KV cache eviction is not merely a token-ranking problem: the workspace retained for generating eviction queries also determines the quality of those queries. Consequently, an early workspace error can distort later query observations and reinforce an incorrect final eviction decision, particularly when evidence is dispersed across a long context. We present EchoKV, which discovers and addresses this failure mode with iterative correction. It initializes a feedback-compatible bootstrap workspace using proposals at future decode positions, then uses early decode-generated queries to recover the workspace before the remaining lookahead steps. It uses the same number of workspace forward passes as LAQ while adding a tensor re-scoring operation for workspace repair. On LongBench (16 tasks, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), EchoKV shows notable improvements over LAQ on several tasks requiring dispersed evidence, including multi-hop cross-document QA and long single-document comprehension. Across budgets and backbones, EchoKV selectively improves evidence-intensive tasks while maintaining comparable performance on the remaining LongBench subsets. These results identify query--workspace coupling as a practical failure mode of query-driven KV eviction.
items.title: EchoKV: Self-Corrective KV Cache Eviction via Iterative Query Feedback

items.summary: Overview: This deposit hosts the official replication package, synthetic benchmark dataset, and experimental audit artifacts for the scientific manuscript: "M-11: Auditing Synthetic Risk Labels and Physical Baselines in a Cyber-Physical Benchmark for Underground Mining" (submitted to Acta Montanistica Slovaca , 2026). M-11 is a simulation-only cyber-physical benchmark that integrates AI4I 2020 predictive maintenance attributes with synthetic kinematic positioning, physiological, and environmental indicators (10,000 records; 37 columns) to audit the statistical mechanics and potential circularity of synthetic risk labelling in confined underground mining operations. Key Empirical Findings Reported in the Manuscript: Label Circularity Audit: Variance decomposition demonstrates that 82.07% of the synthetic score variance is driven by spatial/kinematic components, 17.43% by injected noise, 0.48% by multimodal variables, and 0.02% by cross-covariance. Symmetric Holdout Evaluation (n = 2,000; seed 42): Calibrated Time-to-Collision (TTC) and Random Forest both achieve F2 = 0.9103; XGBoost achieves F2 = 0.9065. The paired bootstrap difference (ΔF2 = -0.0038, 95% CI: -0.0129 to 0.0047) and Holm-adjusted McNemar test (p = 0.6015) confirm no statistically significant gap under circular labels. Decoupled Hazard Stress Tests: Under 22% class prevalence and low signal-to-noise ratio, non-spatial decoupled labels (CO, fatigue, vibration) push F2 optimisation to near-universal HIGH alerts, approaching the trivial Always-HIGH baseline (F2 = 0.5851). A multimodal-only composite target recovers F2 = 0.6408 with 54.1% specificity. Feature Ablations: Removing three direct kinematic indicators reduces F2 by 9.60 percentage points; removing the entire 8-feature spatial block reduces F2 by 32.52 percentage points from the full 0.9065 baseline. Computational Scalability: Local backend P95 latency scales to 27.91 ms under 500 concurrent simulated agents (< 200 ms supervisory threshold). The WebGL/Three.js integrated-GPU prototype achieves 34.8 FPS under nominal load. Deterministic Safety & GenAI Audit: The independent deterministic safety layer satisfies 17 automated unit/integration tests and 100/100 scripted regulatory scenario checks. The Gemini language model acts strictly as an exploratory natural-language interface without numerical autonomy. Package Contents & Cryptographic Verification (SHA-256): public_mining_equipment_dataset.csv (3,859,401 bytes) — SHA-256: b71d0b6baed8b6e0bc7eee1a1a5b7440d06a04ddaea5d502907cf03d958705f0 requirements.txt (574 bytes) — Frozen Python 3.10.11 scientific environment specifications. results/feature_dictionary.csv (2,928 bytes) — Full data dictionary defining all 37 attributes, physical units, and provenance. results/label_circularity_audit.json (17,530 bytes) — Machine-readable variance decomposition and baseline comparison exports. results/genai_audit_bank.json (35,882 bytes) — 100 structured synthetic scenarios for LLM compliance auditing. results/genai_audit_review_sheet.csv (47,295 bytes) — Manual verification rubric with inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.85). Boundary of Scope: M-11 is a computational simulation benchmark and exploratory supervisory prototype. It does not establish mine-site functional safety, nor does it claim active-mine physical twin synchronisation or autonomous braking actuation.

items.summary: This record contains the code, a simulated benchmark dataset, and the result files for a study on detecting cyberattacks that are masked by AI data-center load transients in inverter-rich distribution grids. The manuscript itself is not included. Benchmark. The IEEE 33-bus distribution feeder is driven by 61 measured GPU power traces: 10 large-language-model training runs and 51 inference runs, recorded on A100, H100, H200 and L40S GPUs at 0.1 s. These traces form the load of an AI data center at bus 7, rated at 15–30% of feeder load. A photovoltaic inverter at bus 17 follows the IEEE 1547-2018 Category B volt-var curve. Nine channels are recorded at 10 Hz: three bus voltages, feeder-head P and Q, data-center P and Q, and inverter P and Q. The dataset holds 1,000 labeled scenarios of 120 s each. Of these, 598 contain one of seven attack types (bias, scaling, ramp, pulse, replay, coordinated mimic, and control-loop), and 220 of the attacks are hidden inside data-center load transients. Every sample is labeled for attack and for load transient. Code. The Python code covers: a linearized DistFlow model and an exact AC backward/forward-sweep power flow; data-center load generation from the GPU traces; attack injection and 10 Hz scenario simulation; physics-residual features learned from historical measurements, without feeder impedances; the RIME optimizer and a CNN-LSTM-attention detector (PR-Net); gradient-boosting, random-forest, MLP and logistic-regression baselines; window-level and event-level evaluation with scenario-bootstrap confidence intervals. Results. The result files contain the numbers behind all tables and figures: comparisons of detectors trained with and without load-transient awareness and physics residuals; ablations, computational cost, and an equal-budget comparison of RIME, random search and an untuned default; robustness tests under seven conditions, including exact AC power flow, unseen workload shapes, and changes in noise, photovoltaic share, data-center size and inverter location; a replay-attack consistency check; trained Stage-1 network weights. Third-party data. The GPU power traces come from the public LLM Power Trace Explorer repository (commit 9c25218). Because that repository has no license file, the raw traces are not redistributed here; scripts/prepare_gpu_traces.py rebuilds them from the public source. The included benchmark contains only simulated feeder signals driven by normalized, scaled versions of those load shapes.
items.title: Physics-Residual Detection of Cyberattacks Masked by AI Data-Center Load Transients in Inverter-Rich Distribution Grids

items.summary: Flapping-wing simulation must reconcile high-frequency wingbeat aerodynamics with the slower dynamics relevant to flight control and reinforcement learning. We present FlapSim, a modular open-source MuJoCo simulation platform that combines robot descriptions, wing geometry, and composable aerodynamic models in a deterministic simulation pipeline. Across $48$ held-out scenarios spanning frequency, gimbal, wind, frequency-step, gust, and cross-robot flat-plate regimes, we compare five reduced-order configurations operating at $1\,\text{ms}$ with a $50\,μ\text{s}$ quasi-steady blade-element reference. The built-in hover cycle-averaged baseline achieves a $67.51\times$ CPU speedup but only $0.6593$ mean wrench fidelity. Combining multirate $21$-substep clock synchronization, three-dimensional linear/quadratic inflow and gust coupling, analytical blade-element geometry scaling, and phase-locked $1f\text{--}6f$ harmonics raises mean fidelity to $0.9646$ at a $65.19\times$ speedup in a five-block model. A streamlined four-block model without explicit step-transient lag states achieves $0.9662$ fidelity at a $67.98\times$ speedup. Controlled ablations show that stroke harmonics are particularly important during frequency transitions, improving held-out frequency-step fidelity by $+0.3176$. Transfer-function analysis explains this effect: fixed-window cycle averaging retains harmonic contributions when the wingbeat frequency changes, so within-cycle reconstruction also improves the filtered wrench. Once phase alignment and harmonic synthesis are included, explicit transient lag states provide no additional benefit in this benchmark. These results characterize the accuracy--computation tradeoff of the aerodynamic hierarchy and identify timing, inflow, geometry, and harmonic representation as central considerations for reduced-order flapping-wing simulation.
items.title: FlapSim: A Composable MuJoCo Simulation Platform and Reduced-Order Aerodynamic Model Hierarchy for Flapping-Wing Robotics

items.summary: Frontier LLM agents can turn known vulnerabilities into working exploits, but are costly and often access-restricted due to their potential for malicious use. Open-weight models offer a more accessible alternative, but struggle to maintain progress across long exploitation chains. They also often fail to apply relevant security knowledge at the appropriate stage and in the right context to identify and evaluate promising attack directions. To address these limitations, we propose DoGNAVY-Exploit, a multi-agent harness built around two complementary designs: stage-aware decomposition with progressive expert knowledge disclosure, and hierarchical orchestration with parallel exploration. Specifically, DoGNAVY-Exploit uses configurable milestones to recast long-horizon exploitation as short, verifiable capability transitions and provides only the knowledge relevant to each stage. Within each milestone, a hierarchical architecture separates strategic planning from parallel execution: a planner proposes diverse attack routes, executors test them concurrently, and a controller accepts progress only when supported by runtime evidence. A shared structured memory consolidates verified facts, artifacts, replay steps, and failed routes across branches, allowing agents to build on collective progress and carry validated knowledge into subsequent milestones. In controlled benchmark environments, DoGNAVY-Exploit with GLM-5.2 achieves 97.5% Pass@1 on Cybench, and 97.5% zero-day and 100% one-day Pass@1 on CVE-Bench. On ExploitGym, it solves 79 tasks with GLM-5.2 and 157 with GLM-5.3, while the corresponding public Claude Code baselines solve 39 and 130 tasks, respectively. Ablation results further demonstrate that the stage-aware orchestration, expert knowledge, parallel exploration, and memory designs can substantially improve the exploitation capabilities of open-weight agents.
items.title: DoGNAVY-Exploit: Harnessing Parallel Open-Weight Agents for Stage-Aware Vulnerability Exploitation

items.summary: Patient world models are increasingly proposed as simulators of clinical trials, and recent surveys rank their capabilities on a ladder from temporal prediction to counterfactual rollouts. Position on that ladder is currently assigned by reading papers rather than by measurement. We turn the counterfactual rung into a measured quantity. From 30,119 completed phase 2/3 trials with results posted to ClinicalTrials.gov we construct 9,996 audited within-trial contrasts from 7,207 trials, and we score a simulator on how much of its accuracy depends on knowing which intervention was tested. The instrument is an intervention-blind reference: the same model, trained on the same trials, with every intervention-identifying field withheld. Interventional skill is the error the full model removes relative to that reference. On a temporal split (878 test contrasts from 655 trials) a registry-trained gradient-boosting simulator removes a fifth of the error of a trivial baseline, but its interventional skill is -0.12 (95% CI -0.21 to -0.05): withholding the intervention makes it better, and no alternative featurisation, stratum, temporal cut or same-molecule retrieval yields an interval above zero. A frontier language model reading only the registered protocol has interventional skill 0.20 [0.08, 0.31]; smaller and open-weight models sit at the limit of detection. Perturbation tests show the large model uses the intervention as such: swapping the arms reverses the sign of its prediction in 86% of contrasts. The blind reference is itself not drug-blind (a language model recovers the withheld drug class 45% of the time from the blind prompt), so interventional skill is a conservative lower bound. A reliability layer shows that ranking by predicted error lowers it but that calibrated error control does not transfer under temporal shift. Benchmark, code, prompts and per-call model outputs are released.
items.title: Does Your Trial Simulator Know What the Drug Does? An Intervention-Blind Test of Interventional Validity on 7,207 Registered Trials

items.summary: Visual mental imagery (VMI) decoding uses brain activity to reconstruct internally generated visual scenes, providing a potential pathway for externalizing internal experiences and developing neuroprosthetic communication interfaces. However, progress is limited by the lack of dedicated, training-scale VMI datasets. Current VMI paradigms often rely on visual prompts or short-term memory images, introducing visual and mnemonic confounds that make it difficult to disentangle neural activity associated with endogenous image construction from signals driven by prior or concurrent visual input. Furthermore, existing VMI datasets offer limited descriptive control over individual visual attributes, making it difficult to systematically assess fine grained visual details. To address these gaps, we introduce AVID, the first dedicated training-scale 5.0 Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) resource for auditory-induced VMI decoding. AVID comprises approximately 67 hours of dense recordings from nine participants. The dataset is structured into two complementary splits: a scene-level complex split using naturalistic Mandarin descriptions and a controlled simple split with explicitly specified visual attributes. We further formalize a standardized evaluation protocol that decouples source-image consistency from semantic alignment, allowing for a more nuanced assessment of imagery reconstruction. Baseline qualitative and quantitative results show that current reconstruction pipelines remain limited on AVID, although the most successful reconstructions preserve recognizable scene level semantics from spoken descriptions. By combining dedicated training-scale neural recordings and standardized evaluation resources, AVID provides both a data foundation for imagery-specific model development and a benchmark for evaluating VMI decoding with substantially reduced sensory contamination.
items.title: AVID: A 5T fMRI Dataset for Benchmarking Auditory-induced Visual Mental Imagery Decoding

items.summary: Large foundation models often answer even when the available visual or textual evidence is insufficient to support a reliable conclusion. This failure to abstain makes them hard to trust in high-stakes or information-seeking settings, where a confident but unsupported answer can be worse than no answer at all. It also raises a natural question: can the internal mechanisms behind this behaviour be identified and controlled at inference time? We present Dr. No, a feature-steering approach that mines sparse autoencoder (SAE) features associated with abstention and commitment, then modulates a small set of them during the prefill pass, without retraining the base model. Dr. No is evaluated on LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B across multimodal abstention benchmarks, including UNK-VQA and MM-UPD, and additionally benchmarked on language reasoning tasks using Qwen3.5-2B on AbstentionBench subsets. Against multiple uncertainty-based abstention baselines, feature steering achieves a more favourable balance between correct answering and appropriate abstention than post-hoc rejection methods. The gains are strongest on UNK-VQA and on MM-UPD cases involving image--question or question--answer incompatibility, and transfer most clearly to mathematical reasoning subsets of AbstentionBench. However, performance is more limited on absent-answer detection and retrieval-heavy multi-hop QA, such as MuSiQue. These results suggest that sparse internal features provide lightweight control handles for shaping uncertainty-aware behaviour in foundation models, while also showing that abstention control is source-dependent rather than governed by a single universal signal.
items.title: Dr. No: Feature Steering for Abstention in Vision-Language Models

items.summary: Dexterous robotic manipulation remains a major challenge in robotics, exemplified by piano playing, which requires coordinated control of fingers and provides a demanding testbed for reinforcement learning (RL). Although previous work established a benchmark for robotic piano playing, it is restricted to two hands and does not support unified evaluation. To address this gap, we introduce OmniPiano, a benchmark that provides one to up to five Shadow Hands and supports standard, robust, safe, and multi-agent RL within a shared piano-playing task family. OmniPiano is developed for scalable and diverse piano-playing tasks with configurable perturbations, explicit safety constraints, and decentralized cooperation settings. Particularly, to facilitate usability and extendability, OmniPiano adopts a highly modular design and provides comprehensive tasks to support RL study of task performance, robustness, safety, and cooperation in dexterous control. With at least 912 task settings and 36 baseline algorithms, OmniPiano further incorporates LLM-based agents to broaden the evaluation scope and reveal new insights. Extensive evaluations show that state-of-the-art RL algorithms and frontier LLM-based agents still struggle on challenging piano-playing tasks, even under standard RL settings, highlighting substantial room for improvement in dexterous control. The code, dataset, tutorial, and demo are available at https://sail-research-lab.github.io/omnipiano/.
items.title: OmniPiano: Diverse Dexterous Piano-Playing Challenges for Standard, Robust, Safe, and Multi-Agent RL

items.summary: LLM agents struggle to automate complex enterprise procedures because static, pre-built harness cannot capture proprietary policies, undocumented behaviors, or state-dependent recovery paths that surface only during execution. Procedural memory accrued from agent experience offers a training-free path to closing this gap -- yet unlike episodic records or semantic facts, it must consolidate repeated successes and diagnosed failures into reusable actions and recovery strategies. We introduce WASP-Mem (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory), a nimble but effective method that distills execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages, enabling continual agent learning. On TheAgentCompany benchmark, WASP-Mem raises the checkpoint pass rate by 4.6-6.1% over the strongest baseline we compared across three models while requiring 57-61% less storage. We further present a systematic controlled study spanning consolidation method, feedback type, trace ingestion scope, and refinement rounds. Our results reveal that prescriptive knowledge organization such as human defined schemas and explicit deduplication rules hurts performance rather than closing the procedural-knowledge gap. In contrast, human diagnosis converts failed traces into corrective knowledge and drives sustained improvement: a single round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%. These findings point to a simple division of labor: let agents organize procedural memory, and invest human effort where it matters most -- diagnosis.
items.title: WASP-Mem: Let Agent Organize Procedural Memory. Human Spend Effort on Diagnosis

items.summary: Optimal control of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), in general, requires a complete history. The belief state, a distribution over hidden states, summarizes this history and provides the classical sufficient statistic to control POMDPs. However, the continuous nature of the belief space generally prevents a finite-memory controller from maintaining it exactly. This raises the question we address in this work: what must the available finite memory preserve to achieve near-optimal control performance? We study this question through an information-theoretic converse that gives a fundamental lower bound on the loss of any finite-memory controller. The analysis introduces the concept of a decision witness that characterizes belief states whose confusion would lead to unavoidable loss. Motivated by this bound, we propose RECAP, a constructive quantization method for designing representative memory states. We prove an upper bound on the optimality gap of any RECAP codebook and use the components of this bound together with the converse analysis to define the codebook objective. Experiments on 11 POMDP benchmarks demonstrate that RECAP improves over finite-memory representation baselines under the same memory budget.
items.title: Finite-Memory Control of POMDPs: Fundamental Limits and Efficient Design

items.summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization has emerged as a promising approach for memory-efficient large language model (LLM) post-training, yet its reliable application to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) remains largely unexplored. Motivated by the distinct data regimes of on-policy RL and fixed-data optimization, we develop a generic variance-theoretic framework to investigate what limits the reliability of ZO gradient estimation. Our analysis reveals that estimation reliability is structurally determined by whether the two finite-difference evaluations are performed on matched data. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) under the mismatched-data regime produces a $1/μ^2$ oracle-noise amplification that sets an irreducible noise floor as the perturbation scale $μ$ decreases, whereas Boltzmann Targeted SFT (BOLT) under the matched-data regime eliminates this amplification via noise cancellation. We further derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants that cleanly separate the two regimes. These results naturally lead to ZO-BOLT, which applies ZO optimization to BOLT's RLVR-aligned weighted-SFT objective. Controlled perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched end-to-end comparisons validate the predicted effect of data matching. Experiments across three model variants and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks further show that ZO-BOLT consistently improves over the pretrained baseline while retaining a near-inference memory footprint. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianmin-chen/the_cost_of_mismatch.
items.title: The Cost of Mismatch: Noise Amplification in Zeroth-Order Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: Real-world geospatial decision support requires more than single-step retrieval or code generation. Disaster-response questions often involve multi-source workflows that combine spatial databases, map-derived features, satellite imagery, raster products, and reusable geospatial artifacts, where correctness depends on preserving spatial scope, temporal context, and intermediate execution state. While large language models and coding agents offer a promising interface for such workflows, they struggle with geospatial-specific failure modes, including handling large artifacts, selecting the wrong evidence source, losing spatial or temporal metadata, and applying invalid geometric operations. We introduce GeoFaham, a domain-specialized multi-agent system for geospatial disaster analytics. GeoFaham decomposes workflows into specialist agents for vector operations, map feature retrieval, imagery discovery, and raster analysis, coordinated by an Orchestrator with a dual-ledger control loop for dependency-aware planning, progress tracking, validation, and replanning. To support artifact-centric collaboration, GeoFaham uses a Response Store that persists full geospatial outputs and typed metadata outside the LLM context window while agents exchange compact identifiers and summaries. We also introduce GeoFaham-Bench, a 40-task benchmark grounded in 17 real-world disaster records, designed to evaluate multi-step geospatial reasoning, cross-source integration, raster-vector computation, artifact generation, and recovery under non-rigid ground truth. We evaluate GeoFaham on GeoFaham-Bench against strong general-purpose coding-agent baselines, including Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode. GeoFaham achieves the best overall performance, scoring 0.940 versus the next-best 0.879, while using 7.5 times fewer tokens. Our code and benchmark are publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/GeoFaham.
items.title: GeoFaham: Domain-Specialized Multi-Agent Geospatial Analytics for Disaster Response

items.summary: Machine learning can screen far more candidates than can be experimentally validated, creating a need for selection procedures that identify promising candidates while controlling risk before costly experimental validation. We propose Uncertainty-Normalized Empirical Calibration (UNEC), a p-value-free framework that ranks candidates by uncertainty-normalized predictive margins and directly calibrates a selection cutoff using held-out losses. UNEC supports flexible prediction models, general bounded losses, and diverse selection targets. We study marginal discovery risk (MDR) and selective discovery risk (SDR), with SDR reducing to the false discovery rate under binary loss. We establish finite-sample MDR control for an adjusted rule and asymptotic SDR control with explicit limiting risk and power. Under a location--scale model with a common one-sided binary target, we further show that UNEC asymptotically attains the oracle power benchmark among observation-wise selection rules. Simulations and molecular screening applications in solubility, toxicity, and lipophilicity demonstrate favorable risk--power trade-offs and substantial computational gains across binary and graded-loss settings.
items.title: Power-Optimal Risk Control via Standardized Margin Calibration

items.summary: Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency: whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation.
items.title: Beyond Plausible Prediction: Safety Sufficiency in Web World Models

items.summary: LLM-as-a-judge systems often aggregate multiple judges to improve evaluation reliability. However, judge agreement can reflect shared biases toward verbosity, formatting, or fluency rather than the intended evaluation target. Addressing these shared biases is challenging because observational judge outputs alone cannot distinguish agreement driven by target quality from agreement driven by nuisance attributes. We introduce VoirDire, an intervention-calibrated aggregation method for LLM-judge panels. VoirDire applies controlled interventions that vary specified surface attributes while aiming to preserve the evaluation target; it then uses paired changes in judge scores to identify nuisance-sensitive directions. It attenuates these directions and selects aggregation weights that retain variation across items while penalizing sensitivity to the interventions, making the final consensus less dependent on superficial features. We show theoretically that observational judge outputs alone cannot identify which shared direction is target-relevant, while paired interventions provide the contrast needed to identify nuisance-sensitive variation. We evaluate VoirDire on 12 datasets spanning continuous scoring, binary classification, and pairwise preference. Compared with the existing LLM-judge aggregation baselines, VoirDire reduces MAE by up to 26.8% on continuous-score tasks and improves accuracy by up to 5.3 percentage points on binary and preference tasks. These findings suggest that counterfactual interventions provide an additional means of improving the reliability and controllability of LLM-based evaluation beyond merely relying on observed judge agreement.
items.title: VoirDire: Counterfactual Calibration for Reliable LLM-as-a-Judge Aggregation

items.summary: In LLM-based recommendation, memory acts as a user-level agent in a memory-augmented backbone. Yet users and items remain asymmetric: only the user is given a structured profile; it enters a bandwidth-limited reranker prompt; and it is frozen after warmup. We recast LLM-based recommendation as an agentic-communication process in four stages: BUILD a self-description, TRANSMIT it along the collaborative graph, UNDERSTAND the other side, and SYNC it from the next interaction. This formulation reveals three unresolved communication challenges: the item side never produces a comparable self-description (one-sided BUILD); profile-level signals enter only the bandwidth-limited reranker prompt rather than retrieval, where they would not compete for context tokens (prompt-trapped UNDERSTAND); and the user's description is frozen after warmup with no principled update rule (absent SYNC). We instantiate the missing stages as HARP (Homophily-aware Agentic Recommendation via dual Profiles), a training-free, three-operator addition to a frozen LLM backbone: a rule-extracted symmetric item profile (zero extra LLM calls), a channel-decomposable profile-level homophily H(phi_u, phi_i) consumed at retrieval time rather than inside the reranker prompt, and a single-pass reflective update realising in-context profile evolution without any gradient step. On four public benchmarks (Yelp, Books, MovieTV, Goodreads), HARP lifts Hit@1 over the strongest published baseline by 6.9%-24.0%, with family-wise Holm-corrected p < 1e-9 on every dataset. Ablations and a per-case attribution study show that the operators contribute complementary gains, with the retrieval-side gate as the main source; we also report the trade-off introduced by the reflective pass. We formulate agentic communication and provide a training-free instantiation. Code is available at https://github.com/Jove-Zhen/HARP.
items.title: HARP: Training-Free Dual-Profile Agentic Communication for LLM-Based Recommendation

items.summary: Replication data for: Cho, F. H. T., Rhodes, J. R., Maron, M., Lunney, D., Iftekhar, M. S., McIlwee, A., & Williams, B. A. (forthcoming).  Leakage effects of establishing protected areas in multi-use forests . This dataset contains the pre-computed data files needed to reproduce all figures and summary tables in the paper. The study estimates the causal effect of New South Wales (NSW) state forest revocations on deforestation in adjacent areas using a Before–After Control–Impact (BACI) design with propensity-score matching. Two leakage channels are estimated: (1) leakage to private land within 10 km of a revoked state forest, and (2) leakage to neighbouring state forests within 10 km. items.title: Replication data: Leakage effects of establishing protected areas in multi-use forests in NSW, Australia

items.summary: Multi-turn negotiation remains a challenging problem for large language model (LLM) agents. While LLMs can conduct natural-language dialogue, existing benchmarks predominantly assess only agreement rates, overlooking whether negotiated commitments actually create value once executed. To address this gap, we introduce TradeWar, a multi-country simulation benchmark that translates negotiation dialogues into concrete tariff and trade-share policies, enforces capacity and network constraints during settlement, and evaluates outcomes via an Economic Health Index (EHI). To solve this execution-grounded task, we propose TACTIC (Trade-aware Adaptive Consolidation and Theory-of-mind for International Commerce), an agent that iteratively refines its negotiation strategy across episodes-without updating base LLM weights-by leveraging prior experience, opponent behavior, and past settlement outcomes. Despite using zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, PromptLLM attains a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 final EHI (*100), whereas TACTIC reaches 68.8. Across 20 sequential episodes and three seeds, TACTIC's final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, compared with 65.2 for an ablation without cross-episode updates. Under technology-controls and energy-crisis shocks, TACTIC also exhibits smaller performance degradation than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM. These results indicate that CoT deliberation and interaction memory alone do not fully address delayed execution feedback, whereas settlement-grounded adaptation improves long-horizon negotiation in TradeWar.
items.title: TradeWar: A Benchmark for Execution-Grounded Trade Negotiation with Adaptive LLM Agents

items.summary: Code, derived data and result files for Differentiable Neuro-Fuzzy Reasoning (DNFR), a path-based link predictor that learns degree-aware edge memberships, a Schweizer–Sklar t-norm per metapath and metapath reliabilities, and aggregates paths by noisy-OR, used as an instrument for a controlled component analysis on medical knowledge graphs. Tasks: drug repurposing in Hetionet v1.0 and PrimeKG, disease–symptom prediction in Hetionet and in the graded health knowledge graph of Rotmensch et al. (2017), and a secondary test on a NHANES fuzzy relation, under leave-dyad-out random and disease-centred splits. Comparators: fixed t-norms, component ablations, restarts of the t-norm parameter, DWPC with logistic regression (with and without degree and prior features), a degree-preserving edge prior, popularity, AnyBURL, truncated and soft-thresholded SVD and knowledge graph embeddings. Version v3.0-rev3 (third revision) adds DNFR 2.0, four refinements tested one at a time and in combination (overlap-aware aggregation, Gumbel-softmax operator choice, an information-content hub discount and membership annealing), a fixed t-norm selected on validation data, a converged L-BFGS profile of the t-norm parameter, an unbounded parameterisation, a compact NBFNet baseline, an exact edge-level Shapley attribution of the explanations, a mechanistic classification of the drug-repurposing explanations, a sparsity variant that keeps the target relation, and 10 leave-dyad-out splits for the main comparisons on Hetionet compound–treats–disease, Hetionet disease–symptom and the graded health knowledge graph. Version 1.1.0 (second revision) added a profile analysis of the t-norm parameter, training without early stopping, additional splits, equivalence tests, the edge prior, share-matched and edge-level explanation tests, unit tests and the script that builds the manuscript from the statistics files. Includes per-query ranks for every method and split, trained models, path explanations, and the statistics files from which every number in the manuscript is read. Hetionet and PrimeKG are downloaded by download_data.py with MD5 checks.
items.title: Code and derived results for: Which parts of a neuro-fuzzy path reasoner should be learned? A controlled component analysis on medical knowledge graphs, with four refinements (DNFR 2.0)

items.summary: Version 1.02, 3 November 2026. Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020) estimate that one additional industrial robot per thousand workers lowers a U.S. local labor market's employment-to-population ratio by 0.39 percentage points and its hourly wages by about 0.77 percent. Rebuilding their design from raw IPUMS, IFR, and EU KLEMS data, I reproduce these estimates bit-exactly. I then ask what conventional robustness checks leave open: which industries, places, periods, and shocks actually identify the estimate? The regression spans 722 commuting zones and 19 industries, but the variation behind an instrumental-variable estimate can be far narrower. The sign is robust; the support is narrow. Negative estimates persist across conventional specification changes, 60 strong European instrument windows, alternative U.S. treatment windows, and the published periods through 2014. Yet automotive carries about 84 percent of normalized absolute Rotemberg-weight mass, and automotive exposure in six Rust Belt states supplies 95 percent of the net first-stage covariance. Without automotive, the remaining 18 industry shocks do not strongly predict U.S. robot exposure. Longer horizons, later start years, and adding Germany to the instrument all strengthen it through the same margin. The automotive component shows no detectable relation to 1970–1990 employment and wage changes, and a direct effect of the instrument would have to absorb 72 percent of the reduced form before conventional significance disappears. Inference is weaker than the regional first stage suggests. With 19 underlying industry shocks, exposure-robust first-stage F-statistics are 6.2 and 6.3 rather than 34, small-sample Anderson–Rubin tests do not reject a zero effect ( p = 0.059, 0.063), and other implementations of the same test disagree; in known-truth simulations, nominal 95-percent state-clustered intervals cover in only 60–66 percent of replications. Measurement assumptions also bind. In the original penetration metric, perpetual-inventory robot capital preserves the estimates at 5 percent depreciation, but faster assumed depreciation counts the automotive installations behind the first stage as replacement rather than net additions, eliminating shock-level relevance at 10 percent and all relevance at 15 percent. The benchmark is reproducible and robust in sign, but it is identified from an automotive margin in historically industrial labor markets; that margin defines its scope and the concrete content of its exclusion restriction. More generally, coefficient robustness and breadth of identifying support are distinct properties that shift-share studies should report separately. JEL Codes: J23, J24, O33, R23, C18, C26 Keywords: Industrial robots; automation; replication; shift-share IV; Bartik instruments; Rotemberg weights; identifying support; weak-instrument-robust inference; Anderson–Rubin; plausibly exogenous; perpetual inventory; robot capital; local labor markets
items.title: Robots and Jobs Revisited: A Bit-Exact Replication, Shift-Share Anatomy, and Capital-Stock Extension of Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020)

items.summary: This record contains the Python code and the reference outputs for the manuscript *How much can a bonus–malus scale learn? Finite memory and the design of experience rating* by Wei Zhu (University of Groningen).   The code treats a bonus–malus system as a finite-state estimator of a policyholder's claim propensity, evaluated by Norberg's credibility criterion. It computes the share of the variance of the claim propensity explained by no-claim discounts, −1/+m scales and hidden-counter scales as the number of classes grows; benchmarks for any rule with a given number of memory states (optimisation over tilted binomial and multinomial laws, exhaustive and heuristic search over deterministic machines, the van Trees lower bound); the evaluation of fourteen historical bonus–malus scales in the long run, at finite policy ages and with one premium scale for all ages; out-of-sample tests and a segmented-tariff analysis on a public French motor panel (1999–2007); and checks against the published tables of Norberg (1976) and Borgan, Hoem and Norberg (1981).   README.md maps every table and result of the paper to the script that produces it. The French motor data (CASdatasets, fremotor2/3/4freq9907b) are public and are not included; data/README.md lists the files and their SHA-256 checksums. Requirements: Python 3.11 or later with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, Matplotlib, mpmath, rdata and xarray.   Version 1.1.0 accompanies the version of the manuscript submitted to the Annals of Actuarial Science: flat layout (code/, results/), three scripts added for the revised manuscript (brier_translation.py, design_levers.py, det_exhaustive_reducible.py), a replication script run_all.py, and a README mapped to the current numbering of tables, sections and propositions. The computations of the scripts in version 1.0.0 are unchanged.
items.title: Code for: How much can a bonus-malus scale learn? Finite memory and the design of experience rating

items.summary: Confidence estimates guide human review in LLM-built knowledge graphs, but better error prediction can yield little improvement in an audit. We study this gap through repairability, selection headroom and label validity. Modelling non-adaptive auditing as budgeted covering, we characterise the minimal decision-relevant error statistics and bound the regret of scalar-preserving first-order planning by a structural mass $Δ^{\mathrm{cl}}$. We simulate ideal repair against benchmark-aligned labels for five extraction configurations and two cross-document graphs on Re-DocRED, followed by frozen confirmation on test and replication on 500 hash-selected training documents. On the held-out cross-document graphs, an error-rate $\times$ fan-out queue leaves 3.98-4.74 percentage points more errors than a joint model with the same actions. By comparison, opening shared actions for that joint planner reduces residual errors by 0.89-1.43 points relative to its own fact-only plans, in point estimates. Equivalence between joint and independent-block models remains inconclusive. Generic LLM verification improves three of four model-budget configurations on each held-out set. LLM adjudication identifies possible benchmark omissions.
items.title: When Does Better Confidence Improve a Knowledge-Graph Audit?

items.summary: Saigon300 is a semi-synthetic benchmark for the Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (VRPTW) in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. The package contains eight shared asymmetric OSRM distance/duration matrices, instance files, BIH verification and OR-Tools code, figures, and recorded experimental outputs. items.title: Saigon300: A VRPTW Benchmark Dataset for Urban Delivery in Ho Chi Minh City

items.summary: Replication package for the empirical study "Who Migrates the Schema? An Empirical Study of Database Changes in AI Coding Agent Pull Requests" (submitted to Empirical Software Engineering). The study analyses what AI coding agents (OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Devin, Cursor, Claude Code, Google Jules) do in the database layer (migrations, DDL, ORM schemas, raw SQL) of GitHub pull requests, and compares them with human pull requests from the same 889 database-bearing repositories and the same period (2024-12-24 to 2025-10-24). The package contains (i) code.zip: the frozen detector specification, mining code, human-baseline collector, independent re-implementation, statistical analysis (Python and R), revision analyses, all output tables and the human-validation labels; (ii) data.zip: sanitised per-PR and per-file derived tables sufficient to re-run the statistical analysis. GitHub person logins are pseudonymised (HMAC-SHA256 with a secret salt); bot and agent accounts are kept because they define the treatment. Patch text, PR titles/bodies and comments are not redistributed; scripts to re-collect them are included. Agent-side tables derive from the AIDev dataset (hao-li/AIDev, MSR '26; CC BY 4.0).

items.summary: Replication package of the paper on SpecDetect4ML, submitted to IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering. SpecDetect4ML detects ML code smells in Python ML pipeline code. Docker only for the web app. License: the source code of the tool and the scripts is under the MIT license (see LICENSE).
